title: Tú vs. Usted
body: Tú is informal: use with young people, friends, and family. Usted is formal (more respectful): use with older people, professionals (teachers, doctors, engineers, lawyers, etc.), and people you don't know. Titles of respect: Don/Doña go before a first name (Don Juan, Doña Carmen); Señor/Señora go before a last name (Señor Gómez, Señora Ceniceros).

title: El alfabeto en español
body: The Spanish alphabet has 27 letters, including Ñ (eñe) which doesn't exist in English. Useful pattern: '¿Cómo se escribe tu nombre?' (How do you spell your name?) -> 'Mi nombre se escribe...' followed by each letter spelled out, e.g. 'erre-o-ese-a-ene-a' = Rosana. See the alphabet vocab cards (tag: alphabet) to drill letter names.

title: Llamarse (reflexive verb pattern)
body: 'Llamarse' literally means 'to call oneself' and is used to introduce yourself. (Yo) me llamo... | (Tú) te llamas... | (Él/Ella/Usted) se llama... | (Ellos/Ellas/Ustedes) se llaman... Example: 'Me llamo Rosana' = 'My name is Rosana' (literally 'I call myself Rosana').

title: Opposites in today's vocab
body: Several of today's words pair up as opposites, which makes them easier to remember together: caro/barato (expensive/inexpensive), cerca/lejos (near/far), arriba/abajo (up/down), fácil/difícil (easy/difficult), rápido/despacio (fast/slow), siempre/nunca (always/never), a veces/a menudo (sometimes/often).
